name: layered-monolith
context: Single deployable application organized into horizontal layers with clear, directional dependencies. Favors local reasoning, simple operations, and coherent transactions over independent deployability and fine-grained scaling.
benefits: Simplicity: Single deployment unit, straightforward operations
Local reasoning: Clear dependency direction makes code easy to understand
Coherent transactions: Strong consistency within request scope
Testability: Each layer independently testable with mocked dependencies
Onboarding speed: Familiar pattern, easy for new developers to understand
Observability: Clear layer boundaries for tracing and monitoring
Clean refactoring: Enforced layer structure limits code pollution
tradeoffs: Horizontal coupling: Cross-cutting changes affect multiple layers when adding features
Scaling limitations: Scales as single unit; cannot scale individual layers independently
Layer discipline required: Developers must respect layer boundaries; violations cause tight coupling
Shared persistence: Database schema coordination required across team
Limited fault isolation: Failures affect entire application
use_cases: Traditional web applications with CRUD operations
Simple domain with few cross-cutting concerns
First step from big ball of mud toward structure
avoid_when: Complex domains where business rules change frequently
Large teams needing strong domain ownership
Systems requiring independent scaling of components
Multiple teams with conflicting release cycles
When domain-driven design is the primary concern
component_types: Presentation Layer: HTTP handling, API contracts, user input validation
Application Layer: Use case orchestration, transaction management, coordination
Domain Layer: Business rules, domain logic, entity state transitions
Infrastructure Layer: Technical concerns, external integrations, persistence
technology_stack: Any MVC framework with ORM support
anti_patterns: Big ball of mud: no internal structure
Layer violation: skipping layers or calling upward
Smart UI: business logic in presentation layer
Anemic domain model: domain objects with no behavior
Database-centric design: logic in stored procedures
design_principles: Strict Layer Direction: Dependencies flow downward only; higher layers never call lower layers upward. Presentation → Application → Domain → Infrastructure
Closed Layers by Default: A layer can only be accessed by the layer directly above it. No shortcuts across layers; prevents tight coupling
Layer Interface Isolation: Each layer exposes its own interface; internal details hidden. Public facade per layer, implementation details private
Transaction Boundaries: Place boundaries in Application layer; one use case = one transaction. Ensures consistency within request scope
Exception Protocol: When inversion is needed (Domain notifying Application), use events/interfaces owned by caller. Document exceptions with ADR, cover with tests

Single Responsibility per Layer: Each layer has one primary concern: Presentation handles HTTP, Application orchestrates use cases, Domain contains business logic, Infrastructure manages external concerns
best_practices: Enforce Layer Discipline: Use architecture tests (fitness functions) to verify layer boundaries are respected and no upward calls occur
Keep Layers Coherent: Each layer should have a clear, single purpose and not become a catch-all for misplaced logic
Use Dependency Inversion: Define repository interfaces in Domain layer; implement in Infrastructure to maintain clean boundaries
Transactional Boundaries: Place transaction management in Application layer: one use case = one transaction
Prefer Events for Cross-Layer Communication: When Domain needs to notify Application, use domain events rather than direct dependencies
Document Layer Exceptions: When narrow exceptions are needed (e.g., read-only projections bypassing Application), record with ADR and cover with tests
Component-Centric Organization: Each business component contains its own slice of layers (Presentation, Application, Domain, Infrastructure) to keep changes local
Schema Evolution: Favor additive changes; keep migrations backward-compatible for one release to enable safe rollbacks
